title: Controlling a stage: the eight activities
blurb: Name the eight controlling a stage activities, say what the project manager does in each and pick the right one for a situation.
question: A project manager discovers that a stage will finish two weeks late, beyond its time tolerance. Which controlling a stage activity should be used, and what does the board receive?

teach.body: Controlling a stage has eight activities, all carried out by the project manager. Three handle work packages (authorize, evaluate status, receive completed). Two monitor and report (evaluate stage status, report highlights). Three deal with problems (capture issues and risks, take corrective action, escalate issues and risks). Group them this way and they are easy to recall and to place in a scenario.

teach.h: The eight activities at a glance
head: Activity
What the PM does
rows: Define the work package, co-create it with the team manager, confirm acceptance, authorize the start
Talk informally with the TM, review checkpoint reports, update the stage plan with actuals and forecasts
Check each product has its required approval; update the product register and stage plan
Compare actual progress with the stage plan
Register each issue or risk, then assess its impact
Find and choose a fix that stays within tolerance
Raise an exception report when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded
Produce the highlight report for the board

teach.caption: Evaluating stage status may show new work is needed, which loops back to authorizing a work package.

teach.h: Authorize a work package: recommended steps
items: Triggers include the start of a new stage and corrective action (new work packages or amendments to existing ones).
Define the work package and build a working relationship with the team manager.
Co-create and review the work package description with the team manager.
Confirm the team manager accepts it, then authorize the work to start.

teach.h: An issue or risk turns up

children.edge: Stage tolerance forecast to be exceeded
children.label: Escalate: exception report

teach.caption: Corrective action is put into effect through the authorize a work package activity.

head: Activity
Role
RACI
teach.caption: Official extracts. In take corrective action, the business layer and project assurance are not involved.

teach.body: Kestrel Housing Association is upgrading 200 flats. Project manager Tomasz Wilk co-creates a kitchen-fitting work package with team manager Grace Obi. Weeks later Grace hands it back complete, but one product lacks sign-off from the building control officer named as its approver in the product description. In receive completed work package, Tomasz makes sure that approval is obtained before updating the product register. He is not the acceptance authority himself.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Corrective action is triggered THROUGH authorize a work package. (2) Capture means register first, then assess, before choosing a response. (3) An exception report is raised in escalate issues and risks only when STAGE tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. (4) Highlight report frequency comes from the communication management approach, not from each checkpoint report.

items: Work package activities: authorize, evaluate status, receive completed.
Monitoring: evaluate stage status; reporting: report highlights.
Problems: capture issues and risks, take corrective action, escalate issues and risks.
PM responsible for report highlights; executive accountable for take corrective action.
Completed products need the approval set out in their product descriptions.

summary: You can now name all eight controlling a stage activities and say which one fits a situation, from co-creating a work package to escalating a forecast breach. You can also recall the key RACI rows for reporting and corrective action.

A.q: Which controlling a stage activity produces the highlight report?
A.why: In report highlights the PM assembles checkpoint reports, project log entries and stage plan changes and produces the highlight report (manual 16.4.8).

whyNot.0: Evaluate stage status compares actual progress with the plan; it feeds the report but does not produce it.
whyNot.2: Escalate issues and risks produces an exception report.
whyNot.3: Evaluate work package status reviews checkpoint reports from team managers.

A.q: In which activity does the project manager register a new issue and then assess its impact before deciding on a course of action?
A.why: Capture issues and risks registers each issue or risk and assesses it before a decision on what to do (manual 16.4.5).

whyNot.0: Take corrective action follows the assessment and selects a fix.
whyNot.1: Evaluate stage status compares actual progress with the stage plan.
whyNot.2: Escalate issues and risks is used when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.

A.q: How is corrective action put into effect in controlling a stage?
options: By authorizing a new or amended work package
By preparing an exception plan for approval
By raising an exception report to the board
By updating the benefits management approach
A.why: Take corrective action selects a solution and triggers it via authorize a work package (manual 16.4.6, 16.4.1).

whyNot.1: Exception plans are prepared in managing a stage boundary when the board asks for one.
whyNot.2: An exception report escalates a forecast breach; it is not corrective action within tolerance.
whyNot.3: The benefits management approach is updated at stage boundaries and closure.

B.q:
Which two statements about controlling a stage activities are correct?
1. The project board authorizes each work package.
2. The PM co-creates and reviews the work package with the team manager.
3. The PM checks each completed product has the approval set out in its product description.
4. Checkpoint reports are produced in the report highlights activity.
B.why: The PM co-creates the work package with the TM (2) and, on receipt, ensures each product has its requisite approval (3) (manual 16.4.1, 16.4.3).

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is false: the PM authorizes work packages, not the board.
whyNot.1: Both are false: the PM authorizes work packages, and checkpoint reports come from team managers.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: team managers produce checkpoint reports; report highlights produces the highlight report.

B.q: During a short call, a team manager tells the project manager that a delivery to her team may slip. Which activity is the PM performing?
B.why: Evaluate work package status includes informal conversations with the team manager to understand any issues or risks with the work package (manual 16.4.2).

whyNot.1: Receive completed work package happens when the work is handed back as finished.
whyNot.2: Report highlights produces the PM's report to the board.
whyNot.3: Authorize a work package agrees and starts the work; it is not progress monitoring.

B.q: How often does the project manager produce highlight reports?
options: Once at the end of each stage
Each time a checkpoint report arrives
As set in the communication management approach
When stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded
B.why: Highlight reports are produced at the frequency documented in the communication management approach, as agreed with the board (manual 16.4.8).

whyNot.0: The end stage report covers the end of a stage; highlight reports are regular, time-driven reports.
whyNot.1: Checkpoint reports feed highlight reports but do not set their frequency.
whyNot.3: A forecast tolerance breach triggers an exception report, not a highlight report.

C.q: The PM forecasts that the stage will exceed its cost tolerance. Which activity applies, and what does the board receive?
options: Take corrective action; a new work package
Escalate issues and risks; an exception report
Capture issues and risks; an end stage report
C.why: A forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated in escalate issues and risks by raising an exception report to the board (manual 16.4.7).

whyNot.0: Corrective action is for problems that can be solved within tolerance.
whyNot.2: A highlight report gives routine status; a forecast breach needs an exception report.
whyNot.3: Capture registers and assesses issues; the end stage report belongs to managing a stage boundary.

C.q: In the take corrective action activity, which role is accountable and which is informed?
options: Senior user accountable; project support informed
C.why: The official RACI for take corrective action makes the executive accountable and project support informed (manual tab 16.2).

whyNot.0: The executive, not the PM, is accountable for this activity.
whyNot.1: Project assurance is not involved in take corrective action.
whyNot.2: The executive, not the senior user, is accountable.

C.q: A team manager hands back a completed work package. One product passed its quality review but has not been signed off by the approver named in its product description. What should the PM do?
options: Approve the product personally as PM
Accept it on the quality review results
Make sure the named approval is obtained
Raise an exception report to the board
C.why: In receive completed work package the PM ensures each product has gained its requisite approval as defined in its product description (manual 16.4.3).

whyNot.0: The PM is unlikely to be the acceptance authority for a specialist product.
whyNot.1: A quality review alone is not enough without the named approval.
whyNot.3: A missing sign-off is not a forecast breach of stage tolerance.

reteach.title: A building site foreman's week
reteach.question: How does a site foreman keep a job on track when several crews are working at once?

blocks.h: Hand out jobs, check them, deal with snags
blocks.body: The foreman agrees each crew's job sheet, checks in with crews, signs off finished work once the inspector approves it, compares the week against the programme and reports to the client every Friday. Snags are logged and assessed; small ones are fixed by reshuffling crews, big ones that will blow the agreed limits go to the client. Those are the eight controlling a stage activities.

head: Foreman does
PRINCE2 activity
rows: Calls client about a big overrun

blocks.text: Reshuffling crews to fix a snag is corrective action, and it is put into effect by issuing a new or amended job sheet: a work package.

explain.body: Authorize a work package (co-create with the TM), evaluate work package status (informal talks, checkpoint reports) and receive completed work package (check approvals).

test.q: Which activity includes co-creating and reviewing the work package with the team manager?
test.why: In authorize a work package the PM co-creates and reviews the work package with the team manager before authorizing the start (manual 16.4.1).

whyNot.0: Evaluate work package status monitors progress after the work has started.
whyNot.1: Take corrective action selects a fix, which is then put into effect through authorize a work package.
whyNot.2: Receive completed work package happens when the work is finished.

explain.body: The PM compares actual progress with the stage plan. Any deviation found here can trigger corrective action or, if tolerance is threatened, escalation.

test.q: What does the project manager compare in the evaluate stage status activity?
options: Actual progress with the stage plan
Work packages with the team plans
test.why: Evaluate stage status compares actual progress against the stage plan, which can trigger corrective action (manual 16.4.4).

whyNot.0: Benefits are reviewed when the business case is updated at stage boundaries and closure.
whyNot.2: Acceptance against criteria is confirmed when products are approved and at closure.
whyNot.3: Team plans belong to team managers in managing product delivery.

explain.body: If the PM can resolve a deviation within stage tolerance, it is corrective action. Only a forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated to the board.

test.q: A deviation can be resolved within stage tolerance. Which activity should the PM use?
test.why: Within stage tolerance the PM resolves deviations through take corrective action (manual 16.4.6).

whyNot.1: Escalation is for a forecast breach of stage tolerance.
whyNot.2: Report highlights informs the board but does not resolve the deviation.
whyNot.3: Receive completed work package handles finished work, not deviations.

explain.body: The PM is responsible for producing the highlight report; team managers, project support and project assurance are consulted.

test.q: Which role is responsible for the report highlights activity?
test.why: The official RACI makes the project manager responsible for report highlights (manual tab 16.2).

whyNot.0: Project support is consulted and may help compile it.
whyNot.1: The team manager is consulted and supplies checkpoint reports.
whyNot.3: Project assurance is consulted, not responsible.
